w: A port before Rome existed, built on a rock outcrop where legend drops Jonah's ship and Andromeda's rock alike. Cedars for Solomon's Temple landed here; Richard the Lionheart and Saladin later signed a truce beneath its walls, and Napoleon sacked it in 1799. Layers on layers, all still walkable.
s: Four thousand years of port, siege and legend
_facts: Ancient Levantine port city, part of Tel Aviv-Yafo, settled as early as the Early Bronze Age
Sits on a naturally elevated rock outcrop on the Mediterranean coast
Biblical port through which Lebanese cedars were imported for Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem
Features in the biblical story of Jonah and the Greek legend of Andromeda
Site of the 1192 Battle of Jaffa and Treaty of Jaffa, a truce between Richard the Lionheart and Saladin
Sacked by Napoleon in the 1799 Siege of Jaffa

w: Four thousand-plus flat-roofed, balconied blocks raised through the 1930s by German Jewish architects who'd fled the Bauhaus school's closure under the Nazis -- the largest concentration of International Style buildings anywhere on earth. UNESCO listed the lot in 2003; walking tours still trace the curves.
_facts: A collection of over 4,000 buildings from the 1930s built in the International Style (Bauhaus) by German Jewish architects who fled the rise of the Nazis
Tel Aviv has the largest number of Bauhaus/International Style buildings of any city in the world
UNESCO proclaimed it a World Cultural Heritage site in 2003
Bauhaus Center Tel Aviv organizes regular architectural tours

n: Anu - Museum of the Jewish People
w: Formerly Beit Hatfutsot, the Diaspora House -- a hundred-million-dollar decade-long rebuild reopened in 2021 as Anu, Hebrew for 'we'. Scale models of vanished synagogues fill one wing, telling the story of Jewish communities scattered and rebuilt across the world, from antiquity to the present.
s: The Diaspora's story, rebuilt for $100 million
_facts: Formerly the Nahum Goldmann Museum of the Jewish Diaspora / Beit Hatfutsot
Located at the center of the Tel Aviv University campus, opposite Ramat Aviv
Reopened March 10, 2021 after a $100 million, decade-long expansion funded by the State of Israel, the Nadav Foundation and private philanthropy
Features the Alfred H. Moses and Family Synagogue Hall with synagogue scale models, added 2016
Presents the history and cultural development of the Jewish people from antiquity to the present
_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anu – Museum of the Jewish People

w: Israel's national theatre and one of the first stages anywhere to perform in Hebrew, anchoring Habima Square in the heart of the city since its founding. A small square, a big claim: reviving a language on stage before it had fully returned to the street.
s: Israel's national stage, Hebrew from day one
_facts: The national theatre of Israel and one of the first Hebrew-language theatres
Located in Habima Square in the center of Tel Aviv

w: A museum built around its own dig: Tel Qasile, twelve stacked layers of settlement unearthed right on the grounds. Elsewhere, pavilions of coins, glass and copper sit beside a planetarium, and craftspeople still work looms, kilns and grinding stones the old way. Archaeology you can walk into.
s: A museum built on top of its own excavation
_facts: Also known as Muza, in the Ramat Aviv neighbourhood, established 1953 as the Haaretz Museum
Exhibition pavilions dedicated to glassware, ceramics, coins, copper and more, plus a planetarium
The 'Man and His Work' wing features live demonstrations of weaving, jewelry and pottery making, grain grinding and bread baking
Tel Qasile, an excavation with 12 distinct layers of culture, sits on the museum grounds

w: Tel Aviv's flagship for modern and contemporary art, Israeli and international alike, gathering the city's collecting instincts under one roof since its earliest days as a Hebrew city with ambitions well beyond its size at the time.
s: Tel Aviv's home for modern and contemporary art
_facts: An art museum in Tel Aviv dedicated to the preservation and display of modern and contemporary art both from Israel and around the world

w: Built between 1916 and 1923 at what was then the northern edge of Arab Jaffa, its slim Ottoman minaret now stands hemmed in by Tel Aviv's beachfront high-rises -- a deliberate collision of eras. The mosque's history runs straight through the fault lines of the Arab-Jewish conflict.
s: Ottoman minaret boxed in by beachfront towers
_facts: Built between 1916 and 1923 at the northern boundary of Arab Jaffa, in Ottoman style
Its history is closely tied to the Arab-Jewish conflict
Located between the Neve Tzedek neighbourhood and the Mediterranean Sea, on the road to Jaffa
Architecture contrasts with the surrounding contemporary high-rises

w: Yehuda Magidovitch's 1926 Art Deco sanctuary once anchored Little Tel Aviv; a 1969 facelift bolted on a Modernist arched facade, and the financial district grew up around it since. The grand hall now hosts weddings more than daily prayer, which moved downstairs long ago.
s: Art Deco sanctuary turned wedding hall
_facts: Orthodox synagogue at 110 Allenby Street, designed by Yehuda Magidovitch, completed 1926 in Art Deco style
Renovated in 1969 with a Modernist facade featuring arches
Once at the heart of Little Tel Aviv, now in the city's business and financial district
Main sanctuary now used mainly for weddings and special occasions; daily services held in a small synagogue on the lower level

w: Founded in 1944, before the state itself existed, and still counted among Israel's leading stages -- now resident at the Tel Aviv Performing Arts Center, still drawing crowds eight decades on.
s: Leading stage since before the state existed
_facts: Established in 1944 in Tel Aviv, one of the leading theatres in Israel
Housed at the Tel Aviv Performing Arts Center

w: Forty-eight families broke ground here in 1883, the first Jewish neighbourhood built outside Jaffa's old walls -- and the seed Tel Aviv grew from. Nobel laureate S.Y. Agnon once lived among its lanes; slated for demolition in the 1970s, public outcry saved it, and it's since gone thoroughly bohemian.
s: The bohemian quarter that started Tel Aviv
_facts: Founded in 1883 by 48 Jewish families led by Shimon Rokach and Aharon Chelouche, the first Jewish neighbourhood built outside old Jaffa
Cultural center of developing Tel Aviv in the early 20th century; residents included Nobel laureate S.Y. Agnon and artist Nachum Gutman
Slated for demolition in the 1970s after years of neglect; public opposition led to restoration
Since the 1990s has become bohemian and fashionable, with historic buildings, artisan workshops, shops and cafes
